stem: Jacqui attends a follow-up outpatient clinic with her mother. She had a hospital admission in the context of hearing voices and feeling persecuted, and has been followed up in the community. Jacqui and her mother want to know whether a diagnosis of schizophrenia has been made. According to the DSM, which of the following criteria relating to duration of symptoms is necessary for a diagnosis of schizophrenia to be made?
options: Duration of four weeks of any psychotic symptom as a minimum
Duration of one year, with at least six months of characteristic symptoms (e.g. delusions,
Duration of two weeks of characteristic symptoms (e.g. delusions, hallucinations etc)
Duration of six months, with at least one month of characteristic symptoms (e.g. delusions, hallucinations etc)
Duration of two years, with at least six months of characteristic symptoms (e.g.
correctAnswer: Duration of six months, with at least one month of characteristic symptoms (e.g. delusions, hallucinations etc)
explanation: This has been retained in DSM-V

stem: Kieran is a 33-year-old man who describes to you the way in which the role of alcohol in his life is causing him to feel ashamed and upset. He tends to drink alcohol erratically, sometimes to excess, and this has led to arguments with his girlfriend, and one trip to A&E last month to suture a laceration sustained after a fall whilst intoxicated. According to the ICD-10, what is most fitting diagnosis for what Kieran is describing?
explanation: This is a pattern of psychoactive substance use that is causing damage to health, which may be physical or mental. It is not to be diagnosed if dependence syndrome, a psychotic disorder, or another specific form of drug or alcohol-related disorder is present.

stem: Mrs Jane Andrews is 27 weeks pregnant when her husband begins to exhibit symptoms of tiredness, nausea and abdominal swelling. Which of the following categories does this represent?
explanation: Couvade syndrome is the phenomena of the partner of a pregnant woman experiencing pregnancy-related symptoms. It is described as a conversion disorder. The symptoms are not feigned and are usually recognised as unusual. They are not psychotic in nature.

stem: Hallucinations are usually associated with schizophrenia but are recognised as occurring in other mental disorders. According to community surveys, which of the following is the most common cause of hallucinations?
explanation:
Fortuyn et al (2009) found that around half of patients with narcolepsy experienced troublesome and pervasive hypnagogic hallucinations during daytime hours. Hallucinations occur in other disorders with a prevalence of between 11-24%, with the estimated frequency

in emotionally unstable personality disorder being 13.7 (Ref: Kelleher and DeVyler, 2017).

stem: Numerous studies have been performed regarding the prognosis of people with Bipolar Affective Disorder. Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Some studies estimate that up to 25% of people with bipolar disorder will commit suicide
Within 2 years 50% of patients with mania will have another episode of illness.
Rapid-cycling is associated with a worse prognosis.
Episodes reduce in frequency with age?
The time interval between episodes becomes less with age
correctAnswer: Episodes reduce in frequency with age?
explanation: Episodes become more frequent with increasing age and are often more difficult to treat.

stem: You are interviewing 83-year-old Mrs Adams on one of the acute medical wards, at the request of the physicians. She has been presenting as confused. As part of you assessment you conduct a clock-drawing test. Which of the following is not a reason to conduct a clock- drawing test?
options: As an evaluation of cognitive impairment
As a measure of executive functioning
As an evaluation of someone's praxis
As a measure of someone's orientation to time
As an evaluation of visuo-spatial abilities
correctAnswer: As a measure of someone's orientation to time
explanation: The test is not designed to test someone's orientation to time

stem: Ecstasy is commonly used drug of abuse in the UK that can precipitate episodes of mental illness. Which of the following is false of ecstasy?
options: Similarly to LSD, causes serotonin release?
It has more addictive potential than cocaine
It causes a reduction in serotonin levels in the days after use
Similarly to amphetamines, causes dopamine release
correctAnswer: It has more addictive potential than cocaine
explanation: Ecstasy does have the potential for psychological and physical dependence but this is less than cannabis and much less than cocaine. Ecstasy increases the release and slows the reuptake of the neurotransmitters serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine in parts of the brain. It has stimulant and psychedelic effects. It can cause depressive symptoms in the days after use due to a depletion of serotonin.

stem: Which condition is associated with generalised slow spike-and-wave activity?
explanation: Spike-and-wave activity is symmetrical, regular generalised EEG pattern often seen in absence seizures (or petit mal epilepsy). The wave complexes are usually 3-4 Hz. Faster generalised spike-wave activity of >3.5 Hz (usually 4 to 6 Hz) is usually seen in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Asymmetries in the spike-and-wave pattern are often seen in myoclonic epilepsy, which may lead to erroneous diagnosis of a non-generalised seizure.

stem: Tom has been brought to A&E by his flatmate at University because he has been behaving increasingly strangely over the past few days. He's been observed talking to someone, even though there's been no-one in the room with him. When asked who he's talking to, Tom says he's having a conversation with his friend Alan. Even though Alan is currently in a city 65 miles away from Tom, Tom claims to be able to hear him very clearly. What's the best description for the hallucinatory phenomena described by Tom?
explanation: This is known as an extra-campine hallucination, whereby the hallucination is outside the limit of the sensory apparatus (e.g. in Tom's case, it is not possible for him to hear his friend's voice from a distance of 65 miles)

stem: Miriam is a 45-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. You are having a conversation with her, and she becomes distracted, staring out the window. When you ask her what she is looking at, she tells you that she can see herself standing at the bottom of the field outside the window. It is her body, far away. What kind of hallucination is she describing?
explanation: Autoscopic hallucination- It is a type of hallucination, 'seeing one's body at a distance', which may occur in schizophrenia and epilepsy.

stem: Mr John Spikings, an 89-year-old man with cognitive impairment, has been admitted to the old age ward. He tells you, in an agitated way, that his wife Mrs Spikings has been replaced by someone unfamiliar to him, and it's been terrible having to be in the same house as this impostor. The impostor looks identical to his wife, but Mr Spikings is convinced it is not his real wife and has wanted to do nothing with her. What condition does this description refer to?
explanation: Capgras syndrome-This is a disorder in which a person holds a delusion that a friend, spouse, parent etc has been replaced by an identical-looking impostor and occurs in conditions such as schizophrenia, dementia, or as a result of brain injury.

stem: Sunita has been apprehended by the Police and taken to a place of safety. She is extremely distressed, agitated and panic-stricken. When you come to assess her she looks at you, she becomes very frightened and shouts out: 'get away from me! Leave me alone! I want nothing to do with you! I know who you are!' The Police officer tells you she responded in the same way to her. On further questioning, Sunita believes you and the Police officer to be the same person, using a disguise, and that you are trying to capture her in order to torture her. What condition does this description refer to?
explanation: Fregoli Delusion- This is the rare disorder in which a person holds the delusion that different people are in fact a single person who is in disguise or changes appearance. It is often persecutory in nature.

stem: You are seeing David, a 34-year-old man, for a review. His psychotherapist has been in touch with you to update you on his progress. He has been telling her of a tragic fire that occurred when he was 6 years old, in which his family home was burned to the ground. His memory of this event is clear. There is nothing making reference to this event in his notes, so you make further enquiries with two family members, and they confirm that such an event never occurred. David, however, is sure the fire happened. What's the best description for this?
explanation: False memory syndrome is the phenomenon in which a person recalls something that did not occur. It has gained some prominence in legal cases regarding sexual abuse and was first investigated by Janet and Sigmund Freud, in relation to hysteria.

stem: Selina has had a spider phobia since she was a child. It impairs her ability to function, as she avoids any places whereby she might come across a spider: non-urban areas, public places that do not appear spotless. Her greatest fear is having a spider crawl over her face. She agrees to participate in some talking therapy to help her with her phobia. In one session, the therapist gives a very detailed description of a spider crawling across Selina's face. Her task is to withstand the anxiety until it diminishes in intensity. What method is this describing?
explanation: By exposing the patient to the phobic object and preventing the usual escape or avoidance, there is extinction of the usual (maladaptive) anxiety response. This may be done in vivo (flooding) or in imagination (implosion).
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

stem: Two medications have the same efficacy but Drug A is marketed as having a 50% failure rate whilst Drug B is marketed as having a 50% success rate. Drug B is prescribed more frequently. What is this an example of?
explanation: The framing effect is an example of cognitive bias, in which people react to a particular choice in different ways depending on how it is presented; e.g. as a loss or as a gain. It is an effect of the description, labelling, or presentation of a problem or responses to it. In this question, the two frames are merely different ways of describing the same thing. Heuristics are simple, efficient rules which people often use to form judgments and make decisions. The outcome bias is an error made in evaluating the quality of a decision when the outcome of that decision is already known. The Barnum effect is a common psychological phenomenon whereby individuals will give high accuracy ratings to descriptions of their personality that supposedly are tailored specifically to them but that are, in fact, vague and general enough to apply to a wide range of people. The Hawthorne effect is the alteration of behaviour by the subjects of a study due to their awareness of being observed.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: 'Internal salience' is a concept in psychology relating to cognitive processes. Which of the following is the most accurate description of it?
options: Self-motivated desire for an object or action
Yearning for reminders of loved ones or objects
Rating one's own beliefs above factual information
Rating one's own thoughts as being more important than those of others
A belief that a particular object or person is important
correctAnswer: Self-motivated desire for an object or action
explanation: Motivational salience is a cognitive process and a form of attention that motivates, or propels, an individual's behaviour towards or away from a particular object, perceived event, or outcome. This can be driven by external factors, such as encouragement or instruction from a teacher or similar, or internal, from within an individual due to their pre-existing beliefs.

stem: Attention is the process by which:
options: Sensory information is converted into working memory
Iconic information is processed to echoic memory
Short term memory is converted to long term memory
Working memory is converted to short term memory
correctAnswer: Sensory information is converted into working memory
explanation:
Attention is the filter or highlighter of the mind - it takes all the sensory information around us

and filters out most of it. This can be useful in focusing at a task at hand e.g. reading this answer and filtering out all the other information on the page. Equally it can allow us to miss information e.g. focusing on these practice psych questions and you miss your mother/spouse/housemate popping in to ask if you're hungry.

stem: Ms Winters has just joined your team as the new manager. There are some changes that need to be made to the way the team is structured. Ms Winters invited the team to contribute their ideas on how to approach the changes. She supports each team member in influencing the process. What leadership style is this describing?
explanation: By allowing the team members to participate in the change, the challenges can be negotiated with greater ease.

stem: Dr Abdul Khan speaks English at work and enjoys going out for fish and chips with colleagues. When he goes home he speaks Punjabi and wears traditional robes. What form of acculturation does this represent?
explanation: Assimilation - When individuals adopt the cultural norms of a dominant or host culture, over their original culture. Separation - When individuals reject the dominant or host culture in favor of preserving their culture of origin. Integration - When individuals are able to adopt the cultural norms of the dominant or host culture while maintaining their culture of origin. Integration leads to, and is often synonymous with biculturalism. Marginalization - When individuals reject both their culture of origin and the dominant host culture.

stem: Miss Alison Smart attends a dinner party with friends. During this she is constantly looking around to determine if she is behaving appropriately. Which phenomena does this describe?
explanation: Social comparison is the process whereby people reduce uncertainty about their beliefs, abilities, and emotions by comparing themselves with others, especially when objective criteria of evaluation are not readily available. Social perception is the study of how people form impressions of and make inferences about other people. Halo effect is the tendency for an impression created in one area to influence opinion in another area.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: Group therapy is often used to treat depression and anxiety; it also has a role in personality and substance misuse disorders. Which of the following is a therapeutic aspect of group therapy?
explanation: Irvin Yalom proposed a number of factors, 11 of which are termed curative or therapeutic factors or ‘mechanisms of change that occur through an intrinsic interplay of varied guided human experiences’ . These include: instillation of hope, universality, imparting information (feedback), altruism, corrective recapitulation of the primary family group, development of socialisation techniques, imitation of adaptive behaviour, interpersonal learning, group cohesiveness, catharsis, and existential factors Therapeutic factors in group therapy:

stem: Brown and Harris identified certain social factors, which increased the risk of depression. Which of the following is not one of the vulnerability factors they described?
explanation: The Brown and Harris model of depression holds that certain ‘vulnerability factors’ – namely early maternal loss, lack of a confiding relationship, greater than three children under the age of 14 at home, and lack of paid employment – can interact with ‘provoking agents’ to increase the risk of depression for women. More recent studies support the lack of a confiding relationship as a risk factor for depression. Physical illness can be associated with depression but Brown and Harris did not identify this.
reference: Patten SB. Are the Brown and Harris" vulnerability factors" risk factors for depression?. Journal of Psychiatry and Neuroscience. 1991 Dec;16(5):267. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 254.

stem: Which of the following techniques is employed in the assessment of temporal course of improvement of symptoms in patients with both PTSD and substance misuse?
explanation: The Impact of Events scale has been used to measure temporal improvement in patients with PTSD and alcohol dependence. This was along with the Clinician Administered PTSD scale, Civilian Mississippi scale for PTSD and Time Line follow back.

stem: Group therapy is felt to have particular advantages over other forms of psychotherapy. Which of the following is an important advantage associated with group therapy?
options: Members of the group can imitate the therapist
The therapist can control all the interpretations made
It can instil hope in members of the group
correctAnswer: It can instil hope in members of the group
explanation: In a mixed group that has members at various stages of development or recovery, a member can be inspired and encouraged by another member who has overcome the problems with which they are still struggling. Group therapy is generally recognised as having more intense and rapidly expressed transference due to the multiple interactions and relationships within the group; this can be used therapeutically. The conversations can be more free-flowing and members will often interpret other's actions or beliefs. Members tend to show imitative behaviour with one another.

stem: 'Social capital' is an important concept in sociology. Which of the following describes it?
options: Commenting on society at individual level
The value placed on an individual by society
The resources an individual contributes to society
Groups rated as more important than individuals
explanation: Social capital is a form of economic and cultural capital in which social networks are central, transactions are marked by reciprocity, trust, and cooperation, and market agents produce goods and services not mainly for themselves, but for a common good. The term generally refers to (a) resources, and the value of these resources, both tangible (public spaces, private property) and intangible ("actors", "human capital", people), (b) the relationships among these resources, and (c) the impact that these relationships have on the resources involved in each relationship, and on larger groups. It is generally seen as a form of capital that produces public goods for a common good. Social capital has been used to explain the improved performance of diverse groups, the growth of entrepreneurial firms, superior managerial performance, enhanced supply chain relations, the value derived from strategic alliances, and the evolution of communities.

stem: Émile Durkheim was a French academic who studied suicide and wrote a seminal book on the topic. Which of the following did he attribute suicide to?
explanation: Durkheim proposed 4 distinct types of suicide. Egoistic suicide reflects a prolonged sense of not belonging, of not being integrated in a community. It results from the suicide's sense that s/he has no tether. This absence can give rise to meaninglessness, apathy, melancholy, and depression. Durkheim calls such detachment "excessive individuation". Those individuals who were not sufficiently bound to social groups (and therefore well-defined values, traditions, norms, and goals) were left with little social support or guidance, and were therefore more likely to commit suicide. Durkheim found that suicide occurred more often among unmarried people, especially unmarried men, whom he found had less to bind and connect them to stable social norms and goals.

stem: Cognitive dissonance is often seen in patients and family members during psychiatric clinical practice. Which of the following is the best description of cognitive dissonance?
options: Being influenced by another person's recollection of events
Drawing inferences about others in an illogical fashion.
Holding mutually exclusive beliefs about an object or person.
Seeking information solely to strengthen preconceptions
Holding beliefs that are more pleasant than justified by evidence.
correctAnswer: Holding mutually exclusive beliefs about an object or person.
explanation: Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort experienced by a person who simultaneously holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values; or when performing an action that contradicts existing beliefs, ideas, or values; or when confronted with new information that contradicts existing beliefs, ideas, and values

stem: Rob, a 45-year-old man, attends the GP with low mood and restlessness, which he feels, is due to a mid-life crisis. Which of the following statements is true regarding a mid-life crisis?
options: There is not much evidence to support a mid-life crisis.
A mid-life crisis is a depressive episode that occurs in 74% of adults in mid-life
A mid-life crisis is associated with risky behaviours such as over-spending and
More significant life events (e.g. divorce, changing jobs) happen around mid-life
'Mid-life crisis' was coined by Woody Allen in the film 'Manhattan'
correctAnswer: There is not much evidence to support a mid-life crisis.
explanation: There is not much evidence to support a mid-life crisis. Psychologist Elliot Jacques coined the term 'midlife crisis' in 1965. Research now suggests that the midlife crisis is more a myth and when domains around financial security, cognition and happiness are examined, adults in mid-life generally fair better than their older and younger counterparts. (Ref: http://www.apa.org/monitor/apr03/researchers.aspx)

stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the 'sick role'?
options: The right to relinquish responsibility for their sickness
The desire to seek medical care and advice
The right to be exempt from their usual role
The right to find out the correct diagnosis
correctAnswer: The right to find out the correct diagnosis
explanation: The sick role is a term in medical sociology around sickness and the rights and obligations of the affected. The two rights of the sick role are the right to be exempt from their usual duties/role, the right to relinquish responsibility (i.e. not be held responsible) for their sickness. The two obligations of the sick role include he desire to get better and the desire to seek appropriate medical advice/care.

stem: Individuals reject the dominant or host culture in favour of preserving their culture of origin and are often facilitated by immigration to ethnic enclaves. What form of acculturation does this represent?
explanation: Separation - When individuals reject the dominant or host culture in favor of preserving their culture of origin. Separation is often facilitated by immigration to ethnic enclaves. Rejection is not a recognised form of acculturation. These concepts form the basis of Berry's Acculturation Model.

stem: Paul is observing his son engaged in some thinking. Paul has been reading about Vygotsky's theories of development, and wonders whether his son is engaged in something called 'internal speech', a means of bringing forth ideas, testing out concepts and regulating one's mind, which is different from the external verbalisation of thought. This is the first time Paul has noticed his son engaged in this activity. What age is Paul's son most likely to be?
explanation: Internal speech is developed between the ages of two and seven, and is important in the development of concepts and meanings.

stem: Steven is 15 years old. His parents report that he is becoming increasingly disinterested in family activities, such as weekend outings, or family meals. He frequently requests to go to friend's houses, and it seems more important to him to fit with friends than with his family. What stage of Erikson's stages of development is this describing?
explanation: Ego identity vs role confusion- This is describing the phase, usually during adolescence, when a person begins to seek independence from the family and wish to belong to society, to fit in with peers etc. It is a stage concerned with questioning one's identity, and with learning roles one will occupy as an adult.

stem: Daniel is a male child who is reaching his development milestones as expected. At which age would he be able to speak 40 words?
explanation: Children at 16 months will usually be able to say around 40 words. This increases to around 80-100 words by 24 months.

stem:
Mr Richard Jones is a 40-year-old single man who works in IT. He is polite with his colleagues but does not socialise with them; they have noticed that he reacts minimally to

praise or criticism. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
explanation: Schizoid personality disorder is characterised by a lack of interest in social and romantic relationships, solitary pursuits and a lack of emotional reactivity. Schizotypal personality disorder often involves an odd manner, magical thinking and quasi-psychotic experiences. Dissocial personality disorder is characterised by impulsivity, callousness and breaching rules or laws. Social phobia is typified by anxiety around being judged. Autistic spectrum disorder is characterised by an unusual social manner and repetitive and restricted interests.

stem: Lucy is a 6-year-old girl who often speaks to her favourite doll. She tells her mother that her doll can talk as well. What is this an example of?
explanation: Animism is the belief that objects that are inanimate (not living) have feelings, thoughts, and have the mental characteristics and qualities of living things. Magical thinking is the belief that one's thoughts by themselves can bring about effects in the world or that thinking something corresponds with doing it.

stem: Certain parental, child and social factors make childhood abuse more likely. Which of the following is the least likely risk factor for childhood abuse?
explanation: In terms of parental factors, a history of them being abused or misusing substances increases the risk of them abusing their children. In terms of child-related factors, persistent crying and a younger age increase the risk of abuse.

stem: Who coined the term 'cognitive emotional process'?
explanation: Alfred Alder coined the phrase "cognitive emotional process" when developing the concept of individual psychology.

stem: Tom Briggs is a 3-year-old boy who has been referred to CAMHS with a possible behavioural problem. Which of the following is a sign that he could present with?
explanation: Persistent fighting with others would be viewed as unusual in a 3-year-old child. The other features would be viewed as within the normal range.

stem: Rutter coined the term 'privation'. What does it mean?
options: Innate need to have one primary caregiver
Failure to form attachment to any figure
Separation anxiety from an attachment figure
Anxiety associated with meeting a stranger
correctAnswer: Failure to form attachment to any figure
explanation: Bowlby used maternal deprivation to explain separation/loss of maternal figure as well as failure to develop attachment. Rutter, feeling this was too simplistic, coined the term 'privation' to explain the difference between those who have never formed attachment (privation) and those who formed attachment but lost the attached figure (deprivation).

stem: At what age does attachment behaviour become evident?
explanation: Between 7 and 9 months, the infant shows preferential attachment for a single attachment figure (also known as specific attachment). It is at this point the infant begins to exhibit stranger fear and separation anxiety.

stem: Identify the term that refers to an object or image that an individual unconsciously uses to represent repressed thoughts, feelings, or impulses.
explanation: Symbolism refers to an object or image that an individual unconsciously uses to represent repressed thoughts, feelings, or impulses. Artificialism is a term coined by Jean Piaget that refers to the religiously-oriented perspective that all things were created by an intelligent entity that has complete control over their qualities, movements, and behaviours. In children it often involves them believing that naturally occurring objects, such as mountains and clouds, are man-made. Egocentricity is a child's inability to see a situation from another person's point of view.

stem: Which statement is most true regarding adolescents?
options: Adolescents prefer to discuss sexual and personal issues with peers rather than parents
Adolescents prefer face-to-face interactions rather than via text (through smartphones
Adolescents prefer to discuss career options with peers rather than parents
Adolescents prefer to discuss career options with peers rather than teachers
Adolescents prefer to discuss sexual and personal issues with teachers rather than
correctAnswer: Adolescents prefer to discuss sexual and personal issues with peers rather than parents
explanation: Adolescents prefer to discuss sexual and personal issues with peers rather than parents Studies (such as the one cited below) suggest adolescents prefer to discuss sexuality and reproductive health with their peers as they feel their parents may not have enough knowledge on the subject or that it may be embarrassing. (Ref: Yadeta, T., Bedane, H. and Tura, A. (2014). Factors Affecting Parent-Adolescent Discussion on Reproductive Health Issues in Harar, Eastern Ethiopia: A Cross-Sectional Study. Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2014, pp.1-7)

stem:
Measurement tools used in older subjects Choose the most appropriate tool for each of the following situations in older subjects with cognitive impairment; 1. Monitoring cognitive decline (choose 2 options)

2. Monitoring decline in function of ADLs

3. Monitoring depression (choose 2 options)
correctAnswer: Monitoring cognitive decline: MOCA and CAMCOG Monitoring decline in function of ADLs: MOHOST Monitoring depression: Hamilton Rating Scale and MADRS
explanation: 1) There are many tools for measuring aspects of cognition, function and mental state in Alzheimer's disease. Though not the most sensitive/specific, the most commonly used tool to measure cognitive decline is the MMSE, however, that is not an option here. The MOCA and CAMCOG are two appropriate tools to assess cognition. The AMTS would not be sensitive enough to pick up cognitive decline, and the clock-drawing test and FAB, though assessing some aspects, are not general enough. 2) For assessment of activities of daily living, the OT department have many tools. The association don't endorse one specific tool above all in Alzheimer's but note that some aspects of each tool may need to be modified. From this list, the MOHOST is the only assessment of ADLs included. The BEHAVE-AD is an assessment of behaviour in Alzheimer's disease. 3) The MADRS and Hamilton Rating scales are both used to assess for depression in the elderly.

stem:
Electrolyte abnormality What electrolyte abnormality could be expected in each of the following situations? 1. Rani, a 52-year-old woman under the oncologists for breast cancer complains of being

excessively thirsty.

2. Jay, a 22-year-old man, was brought into A&E in a coma. His friend Josh said that they had been at a rave where he thinks Jay may have taken something. He describes Jay as being very chatty and overfamiliar. He said that because Jay had a lot of alcohol before, his

friends encouraged him to drink lots of water to sober up.

3. Lena, a 19-year-old woman, is under her GP for low mood. In the past she suffered from bulimia and struggles with her weight. Her boyfriend broke up with her a few days ago. Her friend Jess brings her to A&E as Jess noticed Lena was a little confused. She also has a

tremor and some numbness and is dizzy.
explanation: 1) Hypercalcaemia - polydipsia is a common symptom of hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia is relatively common in cancer (20-30% of cancer patients develop hypercalcaemia). The most common cancers associated with hypercalcaemia are breast and lung cancer, and multiple myeloma. 2) Hyponatraemia - Jay has likely taken MDMA which results in chatty and overfamiliar behaviour, and excessive thirst. He has developed hyponatreamia secondary to over-drinking water due to this excessive thirst. MDMA also causes syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) which contributes to hyponatremia. 3) Metabolic alkalosis - metabolic alkalosis is associated with excessive vomiting. In this case, it is likely that Lena has started to binge and purge following the breakdown of her relationship putting her at risk of developing metabolic alkalosis.

stem:
Movement disorders Choose the movement disorder that matches the description.

1. A man who kicks his wife once as he falls asleep.

2. A man on psychotropic medication for a long time who sleeps badly, wakes with a stiff back in the morning and takes at least 10 minutes to get out of bed.

3. A man who experiences slow writhing movements in peripheral limbs.
explanation: 1) Sleep myoclonus/hypnic jerk is an involuntary twitch that occurs just as a person is beginning to fall asleep 2) Parkinsonism is associated with antipsychotic medication resulting in stiffness, bradykinesia and tremor 3) Athetosis is slow involuntary writing movements of the limbs caused by degeneration of the basal ganglia, as seen in Huntington's disease. It can also be secondary to stroke or trauma.

stem:
Personality disorder If all the general criteria for a personality disorder were met, what personality disorder would the traits described in these vignettes be indicative of? 1. Mr Whitaker is berated by some of his acquaintances for holding onto money very tightly. He claims he has to hold onto it for future catastrophies, and will never offer to pay for someone else's drink. He is regarded as miserly and uptight.

2. Liliana is often at the centre of any party, and cannot bear to be overlooked or ignored. She makes sure she's the centre of attention by wearing provocative clothes, laughing loudly and talking copiously and vivaciously.

3. Mike always seems to have several girlfriends, often at the same time. They find him attractive and seductive, and he impresses them with his stories of evading the law for his own profit. The relationships don't last long and Mike doesn't seem bothered when they

come to an end.

4. Nathan demonstrates the self-perception of being unique and superior to his peers.

5. Mary is persistently unreliable at work and has poor control of her finances.
explanation: 1) Anankastic personality disorder: Traits include a preoccupation with orderliness and control (including over money), at the expense of flexibility. Rules are very rigidly maintained. 2) Histrionic personality disorder: Traits include excessive attention-seeking emotions including inappropriately seductive behaviour. 3) Antisocial personality disorder: Traits include ease on forming relationships, but not keeping them, superficial charm, lack of remorse for criminal or law-breaking activity, disregard for the rights of others. 4) Narcissistic personality disorder can be recognised by elevated sense of importance and significance compared to others. 5) Emotionally unstable personality disorder usually involves marked impulsivity and a desultory approach to life; this usually leads to difficulties with finances and at work.

stem:
Developmental milestones (Language) Identify the age at which children should reach the following milestones in language development (3 questions) 1. Develops intonation and babbles as though speaking, but does not say words.

2. Uses 3-4 words together, and can change the order of words to make questions.

3. Understands puns and jokes.
correctAnswer: Develops intonation and babbling: 6-12 months Uses 3-4 words together: 2-3 years Understands puns and jokes: 6-7 years
explanation: 1) 6-12 months: Babbling (consonant-vowel combinations) and responds when spoken to. 2) 2-3 years: By 3 years, children start using 3 to 4 word sentences with verbs that are generally understood by all adults. At this stage the 'wh' are common (who, why, where) 3) 6-7 years: Understands common idioms. Understands puns, humour

stem:
Theme- Memory Match the following descriptions with the correct type of memory described

1. Remembering how to eat breakfast.

2. Remembering what you ate for breakfast.

3. Remembering what breakfast is.

4. Remembering after you have eaten breakfast that you need to pick up more cereal on

your way home from work.

5. Remembering that after breakfast you took your bike out and cycled your usual route to

work, and this felt tedious.
explanation:
1) Procedural memory, or 'knowing how', is the unconscious memory of skills and how to do things. It is acquired through repetition and practice. 2) Declarative memory is memory of facts and events that can be consciously recalled (also known as explicit memory). 3) Semantic memory is a structured record of meanings, concepts, facts, knowledge about the world; it's to do with general factual knowledge that is shared with others, independent of personal experience. 4) Prospective memory refers to that which needs to be remembered in the future, and may be defined as 'remembering to remember'; it can be either event-based or time-based, and is often triggered by a cue (e.g. finishing breakfast). 5) Episodic memory refers to experiences and specific events in time in serial form, from which we can reconstruct the actual events that took place in our lives; it is the memory of autobiographical events, and has an emotional charge.
